lines.text: Ola is twenty-four. She has Long QT syndrome. Her heart takes a little longer to recharge between beats. Doctors call it a long QT interval. Yesterday, her doctor gave her a common antibiotic. For Ola, that one pill could be enough to stop her heart.
She is one in two thousand. In the US alone, Long QT takes up to four thousand lives a year. For one in ten, the first sign is cardiac arrest. Most of these deaths are preventable.
Meet Celia.ai. A heart-safety companion you can talk to.
The doctor gave me Klacid for a sinus infection.
Klacid is clarithromycin. It's on the known-risk list, so please don't start it before you talk to your doctor.
The verdict comes from fixed medical data. The AI only explains it.
Or scan the box. Sixty-eight thousand Polish packs, checked right on the phone.
Your watch keeps an eye on your heart rate. When it climbs while you're resting, the agent checks in.
And if you can't answer, it speaks for you. In thirteen languages.
Before a doctor's visit, it writes the brief: what happened, which medicines were flagged, and what to ask. At the pharmacy, one card says it all.
It's built natively on HarmonyOS. Ask Celia by voice, from anywhere. And your watch and phone work as one.
The safety core runs on your phone. And you see everything that leaves it.
Four million people live with Long QT. We start in Poland, then Europe. Safety stays free. Families and clinics pay for the care around it.
Celia.ai. Know before you take it.
Ola has Long QT syndrome. One common antibiotic could stop her heart.
Your watch keeps an eye on your heart rate.
If you can't answer, it speaks for you.
